c01.display: Welcome back to NLP, Simply Explained. This is unit 2, lesson 1: morphology.
c01.spoken: Welcome back to N L P, Simply Explained. This is unit 2, lesson 1: morphology.

c02.display: So far we have cut text into words and tokens. Today we look inside the words themselves.
c02.spoken: So far we have cut text into words and tokens. Today we look inside the words themselves.

c03.display: Here is the idea for today. Words are built from smaller pieces, and each of those pieces carries meaning.
c03.spoken: Here is the idea for today. Words are built from smaller pieces, and each of those pieces carries meaning.

c04.display: Those pieces are called morphemes. A morpheme is the smallest part of a word that still carries meaning.
c04.spoken: Those pieces are called morphemes. A morpheme is the smallest part of a word that still carries meaning.

c05.display: Take the word "unbreakable". It is three morphemes: "un", meaning not; "break"; and "able", meaning it can be done.
c05.spoken: Take the word "unbreakable". It is three morphemes: "un", meaning not; "break"; and "able", meaning it can be done.

c06.display: Think of morphemes as LEGO bricks. A small set of bricks snaps together into thousands of different words.
c06.spoken: Think of morphemes as LEGO bricks. A small set of bricks snaps together into thousands of different words.

c08.display: Free morphemes can stand alone as words of their own, like "break", "cat" or "happy".
c08.spoken: Free morphemes can stand alone as words of their own, like "break", "cat" or "happy".

c09.display: Bound morphemes can't stand alone. They have to attach to another piece, like "un", "able", or the "s" that makes a plural. Most words mix both kinds.
c09.spoken: Bound morphemes can't stand alone. They have to attach to another piece, like "un", "able", or the "s" that makes a plural. Most words mix both kinds.

c10.display: Bound pieces that attach to the front or the back of a word are called affixes. Here are some you use every day.
c10.spoken: Bound pieces that attach to the front or the back of a word are called affixes. Here are some you use every day.

c11.display: "un" goes at the front, so it's a prefix: unhappy.
c11.spoken: "un" goes at the front, so it's a prefix: unhappy.

c12.display: "re" is a prefix too: rebuild means build again.
c12.spoken: "re" is a prefix too: rebuild means build again.

c13.display: At the back, "s" is a suffix that makes a plural: cats.
c13.spoken: At the back, "s" is a suffix that makes a plural: cats.

c14.display: "ness" turns an adjective into a noun: kind becomes kindness.
c14.spoken: "ness" turns an adjective into a noun: kind becomes kindness.

c15.display: And "e d" puts a verb in the past: walk becomes walked.
c15.spoken: And "e d" puts a verb in the past: walk becomes walked.

c16.display: Affixes do one of two jobs, and it helps to keep them apart.
c16.spoken: Affixes do one of two jobs, and it helps to keep them apart.

c17.display: Inflection gives the same word a new form. "walk" and "walked" are the same verb, just in the past. "cat" and "cats" are the same noun, just plural.
c17.spoken: Inflection gives the same word a new form. "walk" and "walked" are the same verb, just in the past. "cat" and "cats" are the same noun, just plural.

c18.display: Derivation builds a different word. "happy" is an adjective, but "happiness" is a new word, a noun. "teach" becomes "teacher": a person, not an action.
c18.spoken: Derivation builds a different word. "happy" is an adjective, but "happiness" is a new word, a noun. "teach" becomes "teacher": a person, not an action.

c19.display: So here's the short version. Inflection changes the form; derivation changes the word.
c19.spoken: So here's the short version. Inflection changes the form; derivation changes the word.

c20.display: In NLP we often want to get back to the root of a word, so that "studies" and "study" count as the same thing. There are two ways to do it.
c20.spoken: In N L P we often want to get back to the root of a word, so that "studies" and "study" count as the same thing. There are two ways to do it.

c21.display: Stemming simply chops endings off by rule. It's fast, but the result isn't always a real word. Lemmatization looks the word up, and returns its dictionary form, called the lemma.
c21.spoken: Stemming simply chops endings off by rule. It's fast, but the result isn't always a real word. Lemmatization looks the word up, and returns its dictionary form, called the lemma.

c22.display: "studies": a common stemmer gives "studi", which isn't a word. Lemmatization gives "study".
c22.spoken: "studies": a common stemmer gives "studi", which isn't a word. Lemmatization gives "study".

c24.display: "better": stemming leaves it alone, but lemmatization knows it's a form of "good".
c24.spoken: "better": stemming leaves it alone, but lemmatization knows it's a form of "good".

c25.display: And "was": stemming chops it to "wa", while lemmatization knows it's a form of "be".
c25.spoken: And "was": stemming chops it to "wa", while lemmatization knows it's a form of "be".

c26.display: So why does NLP care about word parts? Four reasons.
c26.spoken: So why does N L P care about word parts? Four reasons.

c27.display: There are fewer things to learn. Walk, walks, walked and walking all share one root.
c27.spoken: There are fewer things to learn. Walk, walks, walked and walking all share one root.

c28.display: Search gets better. Type "running", and you also find pages that say "run".
c28.spoken: Search gets better. Type "running", and you also find pages that say "run".

c29.display: It helps with new words. Even if "ungoogleable" isn't in the dictionary, its pieces are: un, google, able.
c29.spoken: It helps with new words. Even if "ungoogleable" isn't in the dictionary, its pieces are: un, google, able.

c30.display: And it matters even more in languages like Turkish or Finnish, where one long word can hold what English says in a whole sentence.
c30.spoken: And it matters even more in languages like Turkish or Finnish, where one long word can hold what English says in a whole sentence.

c31.display: Time for a quick quiz. How many morphemes are in the word "unbreakable"?
c31.spoken: Time for a quick quiz. How many morphemes are in the word "unbreakable"?

c32.display: Pause the video and count the pieces.
c32.spoken: Pause the video and count the pieces.

c33.display: The answer is three: "un", "break", and "able". A prefix, a root, and a suffix.
c33.spoken: The answer is three: "un", "break", and "able". A prefix, a root, and a suffix.

c34.display: Let's recap. A morpheme is the smallest piece of a word that carries meaning.
c34.spoken: Let's recap. A morpheme is the smallest piece of a word that carries meaning.

c35.display: Free morphemes can stand alone; bound morphemes have to attach to something.
c35.spoken: Free morphemes can stand alone; bound morphemes have to attach to something.

c36.display: Inflection changes a word's form; derivation builds a new word.
c36.spoken: Inflection changes a word's form; derivation builds a new word.

c37.display: And stemming chops endings by rule, while lemmatization looks up the real root.
c37.spoken: And stemming chops endings by rule, while lemmatization looks up the real root.

c38.spoken: Next lesson: P O S Tagging. How does a computer tell 'book a flight' from 'read a book'?
